Isosceles On Sides

TrianglesCirclesConstructions
Game: Move the corners of a triangle and watch three lines, one from each corner, meet in a single spot.
How to play: Drag A, B or C with a mouse or finger, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Drag D, E or F along its dotted line, then press Check the claim.
Look for the math

Three small isosceles triangles sit on the sides of a bigger triangle. From each big corner, draw a line at right angles to the far side of the small triangle opposite it. The surprise is that the three lines meet at one point, however you drag the picture.

Equal legs make perpendicular bisectors

Point D sits on the perpendicular bisector of BC, so DB = DC. The same goes for EC = EA and FA = FB. Press Show statement to see one, two and three little strokes marking those equal pairs, and right-angle squares where the drawn lines cross EF, FD and DE. You can drag D, E and F along their dotted bisectors, even across a side of the big triangle; A, B and C carry them along.

Three circles turn lines into chords

Draw three circles: one centred at D through B and C, one centred at E through C and A, and one centred at F through A and B. Circles centred at E and F both pass through A, so their common chord goes through A. The chord of two circles is always at right angles to the line joining their centres, here EF. That chord is exactly the line drawn through A. Press Show hint circles to see the three circles and the chords through A, B and C. The far ends of the chords are marked with dots.

The meeting point is the radical centre

Each drawn line is a radical axis of two circles. The three axes of three circles pass through one point, their radical centre P. At P the three powers are equal, for example |P−D|² − DB² = |P−E|² − EC² = |P−F|² − FA². That is why all three perpendiculars pass through P.

The logic test checks this claim on the starting picture, six fixed pictures (including obtuse and right triangles, mixed offsets and side flips) and 700 random ones. It also compares every step with a second transcription of the applet's own bytecode. The claim is true whenever D, E and F are distinct and not in one line; if they are in one line, the three perpendiculars are parallel and no meeting point exists. The original page states the theorem without mentioning that degenerate case, and the port reports it honestly in the status line.

Try dragging E across CA: its circle changes size but the three lines still meet at a new point P.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
